name: Persian Fesenjan Chicken (Walnut-Pomegranate Stew) Bowls
intro_html: Fesenjan is Persian celebration food: chicken simmered in a deep, glossy stew of toasted ground walnuts and tart-sweet pomegranate molasses. It tastes like nothing else on this site. Each bowl carries {{protein}} grams of protein for about ${{cost_ps}} (at everyday cost), which is remarkable for a dish this fancy-sounding.
ingredients_display: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh (Member's Mark): 3 lb (1400 g)
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 3 lb: ~$5.46. Buy 4 lbs: $7.08.
Pomegranate Molasses, 1.25 cups: ~$7.84. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 2 10floz bottles.
Rice, 4 cups dry: ~$1.04. Buy 1 (covers this batch with some left over).
Pantry seasonings (ground turmeric, ground cinnamon, salt, black pepper): ~$0.43. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $25.97 across 14 servings, so roughly $1.86 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $32.29 across 14 servings, roughly $2.31 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $21.47 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $53.76. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost) for fesenjan that a Persian restaurant would serve for $17, assuming your town even has one. This is the rare dish where cooking it yourself is both cheaper and your only option.
shop_smart: Walnuts are the big line by far. Buy them in the baking aisle bags, not the snack aisle, and check the store brand first. Price per ounce swings wildly between the two.
One bottle of pomegranate molasses looks pricey but covers this batch and keeps for a year. Amortized per bowl, it is a rounding error of tang and shine.
Chicken thighs are the right cut and the cheap cut. Breast would cost more and dry out in a long simmer. Skip the upgrade that is a downgrade.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cook the rice: 3.75 cups dry with water per your usual method.
Toast the walnuts in your dry pot over medium heat, stirring, 5 minutes until fragrant. Cool slightly, then grind them fine in a food processor.
Cook the diced onion in the olive oil until golden, then stir in the turmeric and cinnamon for 30 seconds.
Add the chicken thighs cut into chunks and stir 2 to 3 minutes to coat.
Add the ground walnuts and enough water to make a loose sauce, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook low for 30 minutes, stirring so the walnuts do not stick.
Stir in the pomegranate molasses, sugar, salt, and pepper and simmer uncovered 15 to 20 more minutes until the stew is thick and dark and the chicken reads 165 F.
Taste and balance: more molasses for tart, a pinch more sugar for sweet. Serve over the rice.
portion_html: Weigh the full pot of stew, subtract the empty pot number from step 1, and divide by 14, then ladle that weight over even scoops of rice in 14 containers. Every bowl comes in at {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein.

steps: Toast the walnuts, then grind them fine.
Cook onion in oil with turmeric and cinnamon, then add chicken chunks.
Add ground walnuts and water, cover, and simmer 30 minutes.
Stir in pomegranate molasses and sugar and simmer until thick and the chicken reads 165 F.
